question: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressively worsening urinary frequency. He feels the urge to urinate every hour or two, which restricts his daily activities and interferes with his sleep. He has no fever, hematuria, or burning pain on micturition. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include metformin and amlodipine. He does not smoke and drinks 1 to 2 beers daily. His vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Digital rectal examination shows a nontender, firm, symmetrically enlarged prostate with no nodules. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

paths: (Hypertensive disease)-CAUSES->(Lower urinary tract symptoms)-CAUSES->(Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia)
(Hypertensive disease)-CAUSES->(Lower urinary tract symptoms)-CAUSES->(Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia)

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Urinary frequency" -> "No fever, hematuria, or burning pain" -> "No acute infection" -> 80% CHAIN: "Enlarged prostate on digital rectal exam" -> "Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)" -> "Common cause of urinary frequency in older men" -> 85% CHAIN: "Hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus" -> "Increased risk for BPH" -> "Possible contributing factors to urinary symptoms" -> 70% CHAIN: "Current medications: metformin and amlodipine" -> "Unlikely to cause urinary frequency" -> 90% CHAIN: "No abnormalities on abdominal examination" -> "No signs of acute abdominal pathology" -> 80% CHAIN: "Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level" -> "Screening for prostate cancer" -> "Important in the evaluation of prostate enlargement" -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most appropriate next step in management for the 60-year-old man with urinary frequency and an enlarged prostate on digital rectal exam is to perform a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level test to screen for prostate cancer, as it is important in the evaluation of prostate enlargement and can help differentiate between benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and prostate cancer.
analysis: The core medical principle in this case is to differentiate between benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and prostate cancer in a patient with urinary symptoms and an enlarged prostate. Given the enhanced information provided, the most appropriate next step in management is to perform a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level test to screen for prostate cancer. This test can help guide further evaluation and management.
